references.text: Parallel law concerning a slave's eye that is injured - the same principle of release as compensation for permanent damage inflicted on a slave
The principle of retribution: an eye for an eye - the fundamental legal principle upon which this verse is based
Laws regarding the release of Hebrew slaves - context for the rights of slaves in Israelite law
Laws concerning the release of slaves after six years and the command to send them out with gifts
Job acknowledges that slaves have rights against their masters, since both master and slave are created by God
Jesus quotes the principle 'an eye for an eye' and gives a new interpretation about not resisting one who does evil

Both verses are part of the same legal principle in Exodus 21 regarding liability for violence against slaves, where freedom is given as compensation for bodily injury (tooth) or vengeance is required in case of death.
Both verses illustrate the principle that a responsible party must bear the cost to rectify an injustice or harm caused.
Both verses support the law's principles of personal responsibility and restitution when an owner/master neglects their duty and causes harm.
Both verses demonstrate the law's principle that personal freedom is the necessary compensation when a master breaks their fundamental duties or causes bodily injury.
